name: Jawline exposure camera angles

lead: Jawline exposure refers to the photo techniques used to show the jaw more clearly: pushing the chin slightly forward and down, extending the neck a little, turning the jaw toward the light and choosing a camera position that separates the jaw from the neck.

It helps looks in pictures rather than in person: the same face can read with a crisper jaw and less under-chin softness when posed and lit this way. Guidance comes from portrait and headshot photographers.

paras: People practise the chin-forward-and-down pose in a mirror or on camera, place themselves so light falls across the face with the broad side of the jaw shaded, and try camera positions around eye level. Photographers advise keeping the effect small so it does not look strained.
There is no physical risk. Overdoing the neck extension can look unnatural, and photographers' advice on camera height varies.

angle.text: The techniques change how the jaw is shown in an image, not the jaw itself. People use them for profile photos to present the jawline at its clearest.

lead: Jawline exposure camera angles are the posing, lens-position and lighting choices that make the jaw appear more defined in photographs. Portrait photographers describe pushing the chin forward and slightly down, which they say reduces the look of a double chin and sharpens the jaw [1].

Another widely repeated tip is to extend the neck a little to tighten the skin along the jaw, but not so far that it looks turtle-like [2]. Turning the chin toward the light and putting the broad side of the jaw in shadow is said to define its edge [2]. For looksmaxxing, these techniques matter for profile pictures, dating apps and social media, where the image rather than the face is what others see.
infobox: Chin forward and down, neck extension, side lighting

paras: Headshot photographer Peter Hurley advises pushing the chin forward and slightly down, standing tall with shoulders back to lengthen the neck, and using soft, diffused light to bring out facial contours [1]. He also recommends shooting slightly upward from around shoulder height, which he says elongates the neck and emphasises the jaw [1].

Another photography guide suggests slightly extending the neck to tighten the skin along the jawline, and turning the chin toward the light so the broad side of the jaw falls into shadow; it notes that changing the pose alone can noticeably improve the jawline without changing lighting or exposure [2].

Photographers do not agree on camera height. Hurley recommends a slightly low position [1], while other posing guides recommend a camera at or slightly above eye level so the eyes look larger and the chin smaller. The disagreement reflects different goals, such as lengthening the neck versus minimising under-chin fullness.
